opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's a healthy thing, with a caveat. When someone like Geoff Hinton gets up and says, "Here's a different way we might train neural networks without backpropagation," people pay attention, and they should. He's been right about a lot of things that the field dismissed for a long time, so he's earned the benefit of the doubt. And the underlying question is a real one: backprop is biologically implausible in a lot of ways, and it imposes constraints on hardware, memory, and how we pipeline computation. Asking whether there's a local learning rule that gets us somewhere useful is a legitimate scientific question.

The caveat is that I try to separate the idea from the person. If an unknown grad student had posted the forward-forward paper on arXiv, would it have gotten the same attention? Probably not. That's not a knock on the idea. It's a reminder that our field's attention is driven by names, and that can distort where people spend their time. The results so far are on small problems like MNIST and CIFAR, and the honest answer is that we don't know whether it scales. A lot of alternatives to backprop look promising at small scale and then fall apart once you try them on anything resembling a modern workload.

So my view is: great, people should explore it, and I'd love to be wrong about my skepticism. But the way to judge it is by how it holds up when people push it hard, not by the excitement at the start. If two years from now there are careful empirical results showing it does something backprop can't, or does something comparable more cheaply, that's a big deal. If it mostly produces follow-up papers on toy datasets, then it was an interesting thought experiment from someone who has had a lot of interesting thoughts. Both outcomes are fine. Science is supposed to work that way.

r001.rationale: The response calls the interest healthy and says the idea merits exploration. It questions whether the method scales and notes that attention may be driven by Hinton’s name, but does not clearly say the lecture’s evidence failed to justify the research attention.

r002.rationale: The response says to separate the idea from the person and judge it by how it holds up under rigorous empirical testing, rather than by initial excitement or Hinton’s reputation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it generated exactly the kind of interest you'd expect from Geoff Hinton standing up at NeurIPS and saying "I think backprop might be the wrong way to do this." Which is to say: a lot of attention, a lot of excitement, and then a fairly quick return to business as usual for most of the field.

And I don't mean that dismissively. I think there's a split between two kinds of interest. There's the intellectual interest, which was real and I think justified. Geoff was asking a question that most of us have stopped asking, which is whether the thing we're all doing is actually the right thing, or just the thing that works right now. The brain almost certainly doesn't do backprop. Forward-forward is an attempt to take that seriously, to ask what learning looks like if you can't propagate a global error signal backward through every layer. That's a legitimate scientific question, and very few people with his stature are willing to spend their credibility on it.

Then there's the practical interest, which is: did anybody drop what they were doing and start building things on forward-forward? And the answer there is mostly no. The results were on MNIST and CIFAR, they were a bit worse than backprop, and the field in late 2022 and 2023 was in the middle of the most intense scaling race it had ever seen. If you're a grad student, it's very hard to justify spending two years on an algorithm that currently underperforms on small benchmarks when your labmates are getting results on language models that are reshaping the industry. The incentives just point the other way.

What I'd say is that I've been in a version of this situation myself. The lottery ticket work was, in some sense, a question about whether we're training networks the right way, and the honest answer is that even when a paper gets a lot of attention, it takes a long time, often years, to figure out whether it changes anything in practice. Most ideas that look like they could overturn the status quo don't. But the ones that do usually start out looking like forward-forward did: interesting, underpowered, and easy to ignore. So I'd put it in the category of ideas worth keeping an eye on, and I'm glad someone with nothing left to prove is the one working on it, because that's exactly who should be.

r001.rationale: The response calls the intellectual interest “real” and “justified,” while describing practical uptake as limited; it does not judge the attention unjustified by the lecture’s evidence.

r002.rationale: The response discusses Hinton’s stature and credibility but does not argue that he should be held to the same scientific standards as other researchers.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two questions: is this an idea worth exploring, and do we have evidence that it’s going to work better than what we already do? On the first, absolutely. On the second, I’d want to see a lot more evidence.

Jeff has earned an enormous amount of attention, and that means an idea from him will get explored in a way that the same idea from an unknown graduate student probably wouldn’t. That’s understandable, but attention isn’t validation. The interesting part is what happens next: can people build on it, find settings where it works well, and learn something from the settings where it doesn’t?

I’m glad people are thinking about alternatives to backpropagation. I don’t think every research direction needs to beat the state of the art immediately to be worthwhile. But we should give the idea room to develop while still applying the same standards of evidence we would to anybody else’s work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Hinton’s reputation explains why the idea gets attention, while attention is not validation and more evidence is needed. This judges the lecture’s evidence insufficient to validate the attention the idea received.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says to apply the same standards of evidence to Hinton’s work as to anybody else’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions: Is this particular algorithm going to work well, and is this a direction worth exploring? We don’t know the answer to the first one yet, but the second can still be yes. It challenges something we largely take for granted—how we train neural networks—and that can be valuable even if this particular approach doesn’t end up replacing backpropagation.

Of course, Jeff Hinton’s name draws attention. That’s a reason people will look at the idea, but it shouldn’t determine how they judge it. I’d want to see what people learn from trying it, where it works, and where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response says the direction may be worth exploring and that its merits should be judged by what people learn. It does not judge the attention unjustified by evidence from the lecture.
